questions.q: What kind of risk do you take when your product or service is completely new?
a: Market risk, because demand is unknown
Competitive risk, because rivals are established
Financial risk, because funding is scarce
Regulatory risk, because rules are unclear
questions.why: Lesson 1 defines market risk as not knowing whether the world will want and pay for something new.

questions.q: According to the study cited in the summary, which businesses fared better on average?
a: Those that took market risk
Those that took competitive risk
Those with the largest initial funding
Those that copied a proven model
questions.why: Lesson 1 reports that far more market-risk companies reached $100 million in sales than competitive-risk ones.

questions.q: What common approach to self-improvement does the summary call a mistake?
a: Trying to smooth out every weakness
Building on what you already do well
Seeking feedback from your community
Specialising in a single skill early
questions.why: Lesson 2 says chasing a well-rounded profile wastes the strengths you could pair with unmet needs.

questions.q: What does the Hundred-Foot Journey example illustrate?
a: Combining your skill with a local need creates something new
Family businesses rarely survive a move abroad
Traditional cooking beats fusion cuisine
Competition between restaurants helps both sides
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes the family's Indian cooking skills succeeding once paired with the French restaurant's customers.

questions.q: What does the summary say successful careers and companies have in common?
a: They stay curious and adaptable
They pick one path and never deviate
They avoid all forms of risk
They copy whatever the market leader does
questions.why: Lesson 3 says careers are not straight lines and most successful firms end up with a different product or strategy.
